about.title: From a single studio to an index of ventures.
about.desc: Same craft and ownership standards, now spread across seven teams instead of one.
about.copy: Glazni started as a mobile-first software studio in Moscow, building fast, native-feeling Android and iOS apps — plus the websites, desktop tools, and infrastructure around them — for clients across Russia, Germany and the rest of Europe. As that studio grew, the teams around it — marketing, talent, hospitality tech, design, privacy-first computing, and website migration — grew into ventures of their own. Glazni is now the holding company that sits above all of them: still rooted in Moscow, with Berlin as its European hub and remote coverage across the rest of the continent.

meta.title: Phone — Glazni Apps
meta.description: Phone is a Glazni Apps project: a dialer and address book in one app, running fully offline, so calling someone and keeping their details never needs a Google account or a data connection.

hero.title: One app for calls and contacts. Nothing else touches it.
hero.sub: Phone is a dialer and an address book built as a single app, not two. No account to sign in with, no contact sync running in the background, no data leaving the device — dialing a number and looking someone up happen in the same screen, entirely offline.

idea.title: Your dialer and your address book were never meant to be two apps.
idea.p1: Google ships a Phone app and a Contacts app. Fossify does too. So does almost everyone else — two separate apps, two separate permission prompts, and a contact list that has to sync between them to work at all. Phone drops that split entirely: the dialer, the call log and the full contact list live in one app, so adding a number, naming it and calling it happen without switching screens.
idea.p2: It also runs completely offline. No account, no cloud contact sync, nothing phoning home to Google or anyone else — your contacts and call history stay on the device they're stored on, which is the whole point if you're trying to degoogle a phone rather than just rearrange which company holds the same data.
idea.frameSub: Combined dialer and contact screen goes here

how.desc: No second app to install, sign into or keep in sync.

meta.title: Contacts Exporter — Glazni Apps
meta.description: Contacts Exporter is a Glazni Apps project: pull every contact off your phone into a plain CSV file you own, so switching phones never means losing them — or needing Google to carry them for you.

hero.title: Every contact, out of Google and into a file you actually own.
hero.sub: Contacts Exporter does one job: read every contact stored on your phone and turn it into a plain CSV file, saved locally. No account to create, no cloud sync to trust, nothing left behind in someone else's database. Next time you switch phones — or ecosystems entirely — your contacts move with you, not with a login.

idea.title: Your address book shouldn't only exist inside someone else's account.
idea.p1: For most people, "backing up contacts" quietly means "trusting Google to keep them forever." That's fine right up until you want to leave — a new phone, a new operating system, a decision to de-Google — and discover your own address book was never really a file you could just take with you.
idea.p2: Contacts Exporter fixes that by producing the most boring, portable format there is: a CSV. Names, numbers, emails — one row per contact, readable by literally anything, forever. It's not trying to replace Google Contacts. It's just making sure you don't need it to.

how.title: Three steps, no account required
how.desc: The app never phones home with your address book — the whole point is that it doesn't have to.

steps.title: Read
steps.desc: With your permission, the app reads the contacts already stored on your phone — nothing added, nothing changed.

steps.title: Convert
steps.desc: Every contact becomes a row in a clean CSV file: name, numbers, emails and the rest, laid out plainly.

steps.title: Keep
steps.desc: Save the file locally, back it up wherever you like, or import it straight into your next phone — with or without Google in the middle.

meta.title: Background Changer — Glazni Apps
meta.description: Background Changer is a Glazni Apps project: a wallpaper that shifts with morning, evening and night, cycling through your own collection automatically.

hero.title: A wallpaper that knows what time it is.
hero.sub: Background Changer swaps your wallpaper as the day moves — morning, evening, night — so your phone looks like itself at 8am and 8pm without you touching a setting. Add your own collection and it keeps circling through it, timed to the day.

idea.title: Set it once, and your wallpaper does the rest.
idea.p1: Most phones show the same static wallpaper whether it's sunrise or midnight. Background Changer treats the wallpaper as something that should move with the day — brighter, warmer tones in the morning, something calmer once it's dark.
idea.p2: Add your own photos or pick from a built-in set, and the app keeps circling through them on its own schedule, tied to morning, evening and night — no manual switching, no third-party widget to babysit.

how.title: Three settings, then it runs itself
how.desc: Build the collection once — the schedule takes it from there.

steps.title: Add
steps.desc: Drop in your own wallpapers, or start from the built-in collection — as many or as few as you want in rotation.

steps.title: Schedule
steps.desc: The app tags each wallpaper for morning, evening or night, and switches automatically as the time of day changes.

steps.title: Circle
steps.desc: Inside each time slot, it keeps cycling through everything you've added, so it never looks the same two days running.

meta.title: Ideas — Glazni Apps
meta.description: Ideas is a Glazni Apps project: start an idea, then drop every note and thought you have on it underneath — one running page per idea, instead of a maze of folders and tags.

hero.title: One idea. Everything you think about it, in one place.
hero.sub: Ideas skips the folders, tags and databases most note apps make you set up first. Start an idea — that's the only structure there is — and every thought you have about it afterward becomes a note stacked underneath that one heading. No filing, no deciding where something belongs. It already belongs.

idea.title: Most note apps make you organize before you've thought anything yet.
idea.p1: The usual note app asks you to pick a notebook, a folder or a tag before you've even written the thought down — so the good ones get lost hunting for the right place to put them. Ideas removes that step. You create one idea, once, as a single heading. Every note you add after that — a line, a link, a half-formed thought at 2am — drops straight underneath it, in order, with nothing else to decide.
idea.p2: There's no second level. Notes don't get their own sub-notes, and ideas don't nest inside other ideas. If a thought belongs to an idea, it goes under that idea's heading and stays there — a running page per idea instead of a tree you have to maintain.
idea.frameSub: An idea with its notes stacked underneath goes here

how.title: Start it, feed it, find it again
how.desc: The whole app is three steps, and the third one is just scrolling.

steps.title: Start an idea
steps.desc: Give it a name and nothing else. That name becomes the one subheading everything about it will live under.

steps.title: Drop in notes
steps.desc: Whenever a thought about it shows up, open the idea and add it as a note. No new screen, no picking a folder — it just gets added to the pile.

steps.title: Come back to it
steps.desc: Open the idea any time and every note is right there, in the order you thought of it — the whole shape of the idea at a glance.

meta.title: Journal — Glazni Apps
meta.description: Journal is a Glazni Apps project: one plain entry a day, dated automatically — no prompts, no streaks, no photo required.

hero.title: A blank page, once a day.
hero.sub: Journal is exactly what it sounds like — a plain text entry, dated automatically, with nothing else asked of you. No mood trackers, no prompts, no streak counter guilting you into writing. Just a place to put down what happened, or what you're thinking, whenever you feel like it.

idea.title: Not everything needs a feature.
idea.p1: Most journaling apps compete on prompts, mood graphs and streaks — extra layers between you and just writing something down. Journal skips all of it. Open the app, there's today's blank entry, and you write in it or you don't.
idea.p2: Entries are plain text, sorted by date, nothing more. Miss a day and there's no broken streak to feel bad about — just an empty day sitting in the timeline, and tomorrow's entry waiting underneath it.

how.title: Three things, that's the whole app
how.desc: No settings to configure before you can start writing.

steps.title: Write
steps.desc: Open the app to today's entry and start typing. It saves as you go — there's no save button to remember.

steps.title: Browse
steps.desc: Every past entry lines up by date underneath, plain text, easy to skim or search back through.

steps.title: Keep
steps.desc: Export the whole journal as a plain text backup any time — it's yours, not locked to the app.

meta.title: Messages — Glazni Apps
meta.description: Messages is a Glazni Apps project: a texting app that runs completely offline, sending and receiving SMS and MMS without a cloud relay or an account attached.

hero.title: Texting that never touches the internet.
hero.sub: Messages sends and receives SMS and MMS straight over your carrier — no cloud relay, no account to sign into, nothing syncing your conversations anywhere else. It runs entirely offline, so what's in a thread stays between the phones sending it.

idea.title: A text is just a text — it shouldn't need a server.
idea.p1: Plenty of messaging apps route ordinary texts through company servers, or hold onto delivery metadata even when the message itself is a plain SMS. Messages doesn't have a server to route through — it talks to your carrier's SMS and MMS network directly, the same way texting has worked for two decades, and nothing about that requires a cloud account.
idea.p2: Like Phone, it's built to run completely offline. No sign-in, no background sync, no message content ever leaving the device except over the network already carrying your calls — which is what makes it a real degoogle replacement rather than a different company holding the same data.

how.title: Nothing between you and the message
how.desc: No account, no relay, no data connection required.

steps.title: Write
steps.desc: Pick a contact — pulled straight from Phone if you're using both — and start a thread the way texting has always worked.

steps.title: Send
steps.desc: Messages go out over SMS or MMS through your carrier directly — no app server in the middle, no data connection needed.

steps.title: Keep
steps.desc: Every thread stays stored on the device, not a cloud backup, so it's there only for as long as you decide to keep it.

meta.title: Photo Journal — Glazni Apps
meta.description: Photo Journal is a Glazni Apps project: one photo a day, building into a visual autobiography — and a record of a life for the people who come looking after you're gone.

hero.title: One photo a day. A life you can actually look back on.
hero.sub: Photo Journal only asks one thing: a single picture, once a day. No captions to write, no streak to keep beyond that. String enough days together and it becomes something a journal rarely manages — a visual autobiography you didn't have to sit down and write, and one day, a way for the people who loved you to see how you actually lived.

idea.title: A single frame is easier to keep than a paragraph.
idea.p1: Most journaling fails for the same reason: the blank page. Photo Journal removes it. Once a day, open the app, take or pick one photo, done. It doesn't ask why the day mattered — most days you won't know until years later, looking back.
idea.p2: Every entry drops into a running timeline, one frame per day, in order. Scroll back a year from now and you're not reading notes about your life — you're looking at it. It's the raw material for an autobiography you never had to write a first draft of.

how.title: Three habits, not a hundred
how.desc: The whole app is small on purpose — the archive is the point, not the features.

steps.title: Capture
steps.desc: Once a day, the app nudges you. Snap a new photo or pick one already on your camera roll — whatever the day actually looked like.

steps.title: Collect
steps.desc: Each entry lines up on a single timeline, oldest to newest. No feed, no likes, no algorithm — just the order you actually lived them in.

steps.title: Keep
steps.desc: Your archive exports as a file you own outright, so it survives app updates, phone changes, and eventually, you — a private legacy, not a platform's growth metric.

idea.p2: Nothing rolls over automatically and nothing nags you. What's left at the end of the day is still there tomorrow, exactly where you left it.
